analysis.one_liner: Extends COVID relief with $1,200 payments, unemployment aid, state and local funding, hazard pay, and eviction protections.
analysis.headline: The House passed the Heroes Act 208-199 in May 2020; the Senate received it, held one hearing, and never voted before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have funded a second, large round of COVID-19 relief in May 2020: direct payments of up to $1,200 per person, expanded unemployment and food assistance, a fund to pay essential workers hazard pay, billions in aid to state and local governments to avoid layoffs and service cuts, money for testing and contact tracing, free COVID treatment without patient cost-sharing, and an extended ban on evictions and foreclosures. The House passed it 208-199, but the Senate never brought it to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had become law, unemployed workers would have gotten extended unemployment benefits; essential workers hazard pay; renters and homeowners protection from eviction and foreclosure; patients free COVID treatment without cost-sharing; and state, local, tribal, and territorial governments roughly $915 billion to cover pandemic costs and lost revenue, protecting government workers from layoffs and residents from service cuts [S2] [S4]. It also expanded paid sick and family leave, nutrition programs like SNAP and WIC, and funding for testing and contact tracing [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Unemployed and essential workers, renters, and states

how_it_helps.text: Provides additional direct payments of up to $1,200 per individual, expands unemployment compensation, paid sick days, and family and medical leave.
Provides $540 billion to states, territories, and tribal governments and $375 billion to cities, counties, and other local governments to cover pandemic costs and lost revenue.
Establishes a fund for pandemic premium pay for essential workers and funds COVID-19 testing, contact tracing, and elimination of cost-sharing for COVID-19 treatment.
Extends and expands the moratorium on certain evictions and foreclosures and creates a $75 billion homeowner assistance fund.
Expands nutrition and food assistance, including $10 billion for SNAP and $1.1 billion for WIC, plus $3 billion for child nutrition programs.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would have been borne by federal taxpayers through borrowing, since the bill was an emergency spending measure funded by the Treasury. Landlords and mortgage servicers would have borne costs from the extended eviction and foreclosure moratorium, and health insurers would have borne the cost of covering COVID treatment without patient cost-sharing [S2]. The federal debt from emergency relief falls on future taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; also landlords and insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriated enormous sums as emergency spending — $540 billion for states, $375 billion for local governments, a $75 billion homeowner fund, $25 billion for the Postal Service, and many other lines — all funded from the Treasury, adding to federal debt that future taxpayers bear [S4]. The widely reported total exceeded $3 trillion.

The House considered the bill under a rule closed to amendments, so no member could modify the measure on the floor; a Republican motion to recommit that would have struck a tax-credit provision failed 198-209 [S6] [S7].

Direct payments and expanded benefits are broad-based and not targeted to those hit hardest, and the bill's provisions touched many programs — from elections to broadband to pension plans — beyond immediate pandemic relief [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: During the spring 2020 spike in unemployment and state budget crises, the bill offered the largest relief package of that period, with direct aid, continued income support, and funding that would have prevented public-sector layoffs. The main cost is the debt from its unprecedented size, and its breadth meant some spending went beyond immediate crisis response. On balance, its stated purpose was direct relief to households and governments during a national emergency, but it never faced a Senate vote, so its merits were never weighed in that chamber.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it in May 2020, the Senate received it and placed it on its calendar, held one small-business hearing in July, and never voted on it before that Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Introduced on May 12, 2020 by Rep. Nita Lowey, the Heroes Act was a broad COVID-19 relief bill covering direct payments, unemployment, state and local aid, health, housing, and many other programs.
The House passed it on May 15, 2020, 208-199: 207 of 233 voting Democrats for, 1 of 196 voting Republicans for; the Republican motion to recommit failed 198-209.
The Senate received the bill May 20, 2020, read it twice, placed it on the calendar under General Orders, and held one hearing in the Small Business Committee on July 23, 2020; no vote ever occurred.
The 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021 with no Senate action on the bill, so it died.
Congress instead enacted a far smaller relief package at the end of 2020, and state and local aid waited until 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of the larger package gained: federal spending stayed far below this bill's scale through 2020. Unemployed workers, renters, essential workers, and state and local governments got less relief than the bill would have provided, with state and local aid not enacted until 2021.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of the large relief package

for.name: Nita Lowey
for.role: Chair, House Appropriations Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced and sponsored the bill in the House.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Declined to schedule any Senate vote on the bill after it was received and placed on the calendar; the Senate held no floor action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Trump administration
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the bill's cost and refused to back it in Senate negotiations that spring.

sides.party_line_note: House passage split almost entirely by party: 207 of 233 voting Democrats for versus 1 of 196 voting Republicans, and the Republican motion to recommit failed 198-209 on party lines [S7] [S8].

industries.note: The bill would have sent $540 billion to states and $375 billion to cities and counties to cover pandemic costs and lost revenue, protecting public workers from layoffs and residents from service cuts [S4].
A dedicated retirement division provided relief to multiemployer and single-employer pension plans facing pandemic-era stress, protecting retirement benefits for union workers and retirees [S4].
The extended and expanded eviction and foreclosure moratorium kept people housed during the pandemic but shifted nonpayment costs to property owners and lenders [S2].
Insurers would have had to cover COVID treatment with no patient cost-sharing, but the bill also directed new federal funding to Medicaid, Medicare, and testing that insurers administer [S2].
The bill provided payments to farmers and relief for livestock, dairy, and specialty crop producers hit by the pandemic [S2] [S4].
A $4 billion emergency broadband benefit and $1.5 billion for school and library connectivity would have routed federal subsidies through internet providers to keep households connected [S4].
